title: Subscriptions and external links help drive resentful users to alternative and extremist YouTube channels
screen_reason: Behavioural browsing study (n = 1,181 US adults, YouGov panel + browser extension, 21 July - 31 December 2020, 1,097,849 video views) that classifies every YouTube video watched by channel type using curated expert source lists, and reports: the share of participants who watched any alternative / extremist channel video (REACH), the share of all videos watched that came from those channels (EXPOSURE), the concentration of that viewing among a tiny group of participants (CONCENTRATION), and mean watch time among viewers (intensity). The source-level typology is the same design the review's 'unreliable or untrustworthy sources' criterion covers - alternative channels are defined as those that 'legitimize discredited views' - and the authors explicitly model it on domain-level content-quality ratings. Flagged borderline: the lists are built on ideology/extremism and 'potential harm' rather than on verified falsity, so a reasonable coder could screen this EXCLUDE as a harmful-content rather than misinformation study.

estimates.platform: YouTube (desktop browser activity logged by a custom Chrome/Firefox extension)
estimates.date: 21 July - 31 December 2020 (median 133 days enrolled per participant)
estimates.measure_type: % of participants who viewed at least one video from an alternative channel
estimates.denominator: 1,181 US participants with browser activity data (YouGov panel: 778 from a nationally representative CCES sample, 97 from a high-resentment oversample, 306 from a heavy-YouTube-user oversample; weighted to be nationally representative)
estimates.definition: At least one logged view of a video from one of the 322 channels on the alternative-channel list
estimates.misinfo_def: In our typology, alternative channels discuss controversial topics through a lens that attempts to legitimize discredited views by casting them as marginalized viewpoints
estimates.source_quote: Only 15.4% (95% CI, 13.4 to 17.5) of the sample for whom we have browser activity data (n = 1181) viewed any video from an alternative channel, and only 6.1% (95% CI, 4.8 to 7.5) viewed any video from an extremist channel.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Curated expert channel lists: 322 alternative channels combining Ledwich & Zaitsev's Men's Rights Activist / Anti-SJW channels (223), Ribeiro et al.'s Intellectual Dark Web and Alt-lite channels (141) and Lewis's Alternative Influence Network (24); 68 appeared on two source lists and 9 on three. Videos from 208 of these channels were actually viewed. No inter-coder reliability (list-based classification)
estimates.moderator_quote: Following studies of information consumption online that rely on ratings of content quality at the domain level (32, 33), we construct a typology of YouTube channel types to measure participant exposure.
estimates.notes: borderline = true for every row in this paper: the channel lists are expert judgments of 'potentially harmful' content (legitimizing discredited views; white identitarian / supremacist / alt-right) rather than lists of sources verified to publish false claims, so the construct sits between untrustworthy-source exposure and harmful-content exposure. Sample is a weighted panel with deliberate oversamples of resentful and heavy-YouTube users - weights are applied but the authors note it 'is of course not fully representative'.

A view-count version of the same statistic is reported (1.9% of participants for 80% of alternative-channel views) - recorded in missed_or_uncertain rather than as a second row.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) View-count versions of the concentration statistics, not given their own rows: '1.9% (95% CI, 0.0 to 5.8) and 1.1% (95% CI, 0.0 to 5.0) of participants were responsible for 80% of alternative and extremist channel viewership, respectively' (fig. S16), and for comparison 3.8% of participants account for 80% of mainstream-media views. An adjudicator wanting them can lift them directly (conc_unit user, conc_dimension exposure). (2) Mainstream-media comparators (43.5% of participants viewed at least one mainstream video; mainstream channels = 3.57% of views; 11.9 min/week) are credible-source measures, not misinformation. (3) Subscription composition of exposure - 60.8% of alternative-channel views and 54.7% of extremist-channel views come from subscribers to that channel (92.9% and 84.7% when counting subscribers to any channel of that type); 51.7% of extremist-channel viewers and 39.0% of alternative-channel viewers watched a video from a channel they subscribed to - are within-misinfo composition shares (denominator is already the harmful-content pool), so not prevalence rows. (4) Rabbit-hole and recommendation statistics are pathway measures, not prevalence of misinformation content: following a recommendation to an alternative/extremist video = 0.17% of all video visits among 7.3% of participants, tightening to 0.01% of visits among 3.0% of participants when all four rabbit-hole criteria are applied (0.002% of visits among 1.0% of participants for extremist endpoints); 47.9% of recommendations shown while watching an alternative-channel video point to another alternative-channel video, 41.1% for extremist; 50.3%/54.3% of recommendations shown and 53.7%/73.8% of recommendations followed from alternative/extremist videos go to alternative or extremist videos. These denominators are recommendations or visits conditional on already consuming the content. (5) Referrer shares (52.4% and 46.6% of referrals to alternative and extremist videos are off-platform; 9.3% of extremist-channel views preceded by an alternative social media site) are pathway composition, not prevalence. (6) Joe Rogan's channel alone accounts for 11.6% of all visits and 26.0% of all time spent on alternative-channel videos - a source-concentration figure within the misinfo pool (conc_unit source would need a stated group %, which is not given as a percentage of sources), so not extracted. (7) ELIGIBILITY CAVEAT: the whole paper hinges on whether 'alternative' and 'extremist' YouTube channels count as untrustworthy sources for this review. I judged yes (alternative channels are defined by legitimizing discredited views, the typology is explicitly modelled on domain-level content-quality ratings, and the mainstream comparison list is filtered on NewsGuard scores and Grinberg et al.'s fake-news lists); a coder who requires a veracity-based source list would screen it EXCLUDE, and every row is marked borderline for that reason.

rob.design: Paired survey + passive browser data. YouGov surveyed 4,000 respondents (2,000 nationally representative 2018 CCES re-contacts, a 1,000-person oversample high in racial resentment / hostile sexism / denial of institutional racism, and a 1,000-person oversample of very frequent YouTube users); 1,181 of them installed a Chrome/Firefox extension (778 / 97 / 306 from the three strata) that passively logged page views and captured HTML snapshots of watched videos, 21 July - 31 December 2020, median enrolment 133 days; 1,097,849 video views and 8,303,137 recommendations. YouGov weights make the extension subsample approximate a national sample, though the authors state it 'is of course not fully representative of the U.S. adult population'. Classification is source-level against curated expert lists (322 alternative, 290 extremist - 36.2% of extremist channels on two or more lists - and 127 mainstream channels screened for NewsGuard > 60 and absence from Grinberg et al.'s fake-news lists); no inter-coder reliability is reported because classification is list-based, the lists are not public, and channels missed by the lists fall into the residual 'other' category. Watch time is inferred from timestamps and capped at video length; the authors note they 'cannot verify that every user saw the content that appeared on their device', and results are framed as a lower bound on rabbit-hole events. Desktop browsers only (no mobile app viewing).
rob.item6_quote: In our typology, alternative channels discuss controversial topics through a lens that attempts to legitimize discredited views by casting them as marginalized viewpoints (despite the channel owners often identifying as white and/or male).
rob.item10_quote: Only 15.4% (95% CI, 13.4 to 17.5) of the sample for whom we have browser activity data (n = 1181) viewed any video from an alternative channel, and only 6.1% (95% CI, 4.8 to 7.5) viewed any video from an extremist channel.
